quoted.text:
Today, there was a statement from the President of the United States that an energy ceasefire has been secured. This is good news for everyone – and it is important that it become reality.

Unfortunately, Ukrainian skies have been infested with Russian “shaheds” all day today. There have been glide bomb strikes and strikes on our energy infrastructure too. A power plant in Kharkiv was attacked this evening.

Overall, this past week alone, the Russians have carried out more than 200 strikes on our electricity generation and transmission facilities in Ukraine, and another 17 strikes this week targeted gas and oil facilities. They have killed more than 150 of our people, and more than 700 people have been wounded.

Ukraine has proposed many de-escalatory steps. Putin had one answer to all of them – “nyet.” We do hope that he will finally say something to America, Ukraine, and the entire world that will lead to a real and dignified peace.

Ukraine wants peace. The question is whether Russia does. The Armed Forces of Ukraine have received all the appropriate orders. We are awaiting clear details of the dialogue between America and Russia – and we expect Putin to follow through on what President Trump said.

ROAD TO 250: Founders Close to Home

Did you know that one of George Washington's Revolutionary War spies was a woman from Long Island?

Anna Smith Strong, of Setauket, is believed to have helped the Culper Spy Ring by hanging laundry on her clothesline to send coded signals about secret meeting locations.

Her story reminds us that the fight for American independence wasn't just waged on battlefields. It happened right here in our own backyard!

text:
September CPI report shows inflation rising, again. This hot CPI report is exhibit number 327 that the policies of trump and Republicans are wrecking our economy.

November is coming. https://t.co/3yPZ40IlJA

quoted.text:
US September CPI:  Inflation arrived hot in September on the back of rising energy prices, transportation costs and consumer electronics all combined to drive the CPI 0.6% higher on the month and 3.7% from one year ago. Core inflation advanced at a 0.3% m/m & 2.6% pace y/y. 

Real average hourly earnings were down 0.1% and declined 0.7% from one year ago. Gasoline prices were up 9.1% and fuel oil 15.3% on the month. Service sector prices increased 0.4% and are up 3.1% from one year ago.  

The topline inflation implies real wages declined for the sixth consecutive month which is intensifying the very real cost of living crisis that a majority of American households are experiencing. 

The September CPI data provided little in the way of disinflation evidence. This points towards more than one additional rate hike from the Fed. 

The problem is not an accelerated broadening out of inflation. The problem is stubborn and sticky inflation that is not going to decline below 3% in topline CPI, PCE or more importantly core PCE anytime soon which will demand a higher policy rate. 

The data, which captures volatile energy, oil and distillate dynamics due to the war in Iran, is likely not sufficient to push the Fed to hike rates at its October meeting. That will wait until December where we see a 25-basis point hike to close out the year.

Smart investments in transportation make a real difference for our communities! We broke ground on the Logan Express Remote Terminal in Braintree, the first permanent remote terminal in the United States.

This project will create a “remote terminal” for Delta and JetBlue passengers in Braintree that will allow passengers to have their baggage screened and complete the entire airport security process before they arrive at Logan Airport, with bus drop-off post-security, enabling them to proceed directly to the departure gate. This Union-built facility will give South Shore residents a convenient way to access Logan Airport while supporting local workers and businesses.

I’m proud to have worked alongside @MassGovernor, @townofbraintree Mayor Erin Joyce,  @Massport CEO Rich Davey, @MBTA Secretary Phil Eng, Senators Bill Driscoll and John Keenan, and Representative Mark Cusack for making this happen. And special thanks to Pat Mulkerrin of the Quincy/South Shore Building Trades and Lou Antonellis of @IBEW103 and the skilled men and women who actually make these projects possible.

Just one more fascinating piece of Long Island history and a reminder that everyday people played extraordinary roles in America's fight for independence!

But if you kill BAAJA now, you’re back at square one—or worse, since you’ll have alienated all the negotiators who secured this deal. 

If/when Dems take the majority, instead of moving forward, you’ll be picking up the pieces of this deal on the pretty thin hope that you can write an entirely new and better one, and somehow get Trump to sign it when he’ll have zero incentive to do so. 

The clear move here—including the best way to set Dems up for success next Congress—is to take this (quite strong) deal and hit the ground running next Congress to do more.

We’re concerned about families being detained without knowledge of their charges, the continued denial of due process, and inadequate access to sanitary food, water, and health services.
 
Regardless of a person’s station in life, they are still human and deserve safe living conditions.
 
We will continue oversight of these facilities until Trump stops weaponizing ICE to harm immigrant families.

text:
It was an honor to recognize Evelyn Margolin of Cameron Ranch Elementary School in Carmichael as our October Educator of the Month!

For 25 years, Evelyn served as a special education teacher in the San Juan Unified School District. Throughout her career, she championed inclusive education, supported families, and helped ensure students of all abilities had the opportunity to succeed.

Even in retirement, she continues to give back through Margolin’s Garden of Learning, a garden she founded where she teaches weekly lessons in science, nutrition, and environmental stewardship to students from transitional kindergarten through fifth grade.

As the son of a public school teacher, I know firsthand the lasting impact that dedicated educators have on our children and communities. 

Thank you, Evelyn, for your decades of service and continued commitment to the next generation of learners!

R…

reposted.text:
The entire point of the certainty provisions in BAAJA is they *DO NOT* rely on a non-binding promise from the admin

Rep Casten's view relies on a popular misconception about how the admin abuses permits: 🧵

– Lots of folks believe the Trump administration is literally ignoring the law to block renewables --> therefore, no change to the law can fix the abuse.

– But this is an exaggeration. The administration is not ignoring courts (or they wouldn't be bothering to ask courts to overturn permits).

– What the admin is doing is using authorities latent in existing law to abuse projects (e.g. refusing to issue permits, using pretexts to revoke permits, etc.). 

– The admin's tactics work where the law doesn't provide clear limits on agency behavior and/or doesn't give sponsors & courts the ability to enforce the law effectively.

– This is a big difference because it means a new law (e.g. BAAJA) can fix the problem by tightening existing authorities, banning misuse, and creating new remedies for courts to enforce the law.

And BAAJA does exactly that! The bill establishes: 

1. Extremely tight limits on agency behavior (limits revocations, requires timeline permit decisions).

2. Creates bold new remedies for project sponsors and courts to enforce the law.

– If the admin tried their current tactics under BAAJA's protections they'd be under siege by lawsuits; project sponsors would have more incentive to sue, be more likely to win, and courts would have far larger remedies to correct abuse.
https://t.co/9BVRH8bW1z

text:
Checking in from a week in the North Coast!

This week, I held a town hall in Gualala for residents from across the Mendocino and Sonoma Coast. 130 people attended, and the discussion was engaged and constructive. Many attendees expressed concern about the Trump administration surging ICE agents into California. Our communities must not become a staging ground for a lawless paramilitary force, and those agents must not be used in any way to interfere with our elections. I was inspired by the positive resolve in the room to take back our democracy.

I also had the opportunity to visit several local projects and organizations:

I toured the construction of the new community center in Gualala. It is part of the community’s plan to rebuild after the arson fire, and it is supported by a million-dollar grant I secured.

I visited the Mendonoma Health Alliance, which is delivering care through a mobile clinic made possible by grant funding.

I visited the Sea Ranch to meet with the North Sonoma Coast Fire Protection District. Its first responders are doing remarkable work to make our community more resilient!

text:
I just returned from my first CODEL to Canada, where I advocated for my California constituents suffering from the president’s tariff wars with our Northern neighbor.  

Canadians have been among our closest allies, fighting side-by-side in both world wars and innumerable other conflicts. 

When Los Angeles was burning, I met countless firefighters who came south to help us battle the blazes and save our homes and lives. 

Sadly, all too many Canadians feel betrayed by the President’s attacks on Canada, his demeaning comments about the country, and the 51st state nonsense. 

More to the point, the tariffs and a resulting Canadian boycott of certain American goods — like California wine — are hurting people on both sides of the border. 

And even if those trade disputes ended tomorrow, the damage will not disappear overnight. 
 
I went to understand more about how we can repair what is already broken, and the pathways to rebuilding an invaluable friendship with our neighbors.

Here’s what I saw:

text:
My first stop was Alberta, the only province not boycotting Californian wines.

I spoke to provincial leaders about the importance of the Canadian market to California farmers and the importance of continuing close collaboration on dairy, beef and energy trade.

There is a political tradition in Canada, as there is in the United States, of politicians serving pancakes to their constituents. It was a pleasure to join Alberta’s Premier, Danielle Smith, for some good food and frank conversation about the needs of farmers in California and Alberta.

I then traveled to Ottawa, the nation's capital, to sit down with Canadian Minister for Agriculture, Heath MacDonald, and members of Parliament to discuss these issues and what can be done to mitigate the harms to both our economies until we can end them. 

The tariff wars are raising costs in the United States on everything from steel and lumber to wine bottles to the potash farmers need for their fertilizer. Between the Canadian tariffs and the war in Iran (components of fertilizer also go through the Strait of Hormuz), the input costs for farmers have gone way up. 

Without American wine on Canadian shelves, Canadians are also missing out on tens of millions of dollars in tax revenue they would obtain from selling our wine.

My first stop was Alberta, the only province not boycotting Californian wines.

I spoke to provincial leaders about the importance of the Canadian market to California farmers and the importance of continuing close collaboration on dairy, beef and energy trade.

There is a political tradition in Canada, as there is in the United States, of politicians serving pancakes to their constituents. It was a pleasure to join Alberta’s Premier, Danielle Smith, for some good food and frank conversation about the needs of farmers in California and Alberta.

text:
I also met with the American Chamber of Commerce in Canada and representatives of American companies impacted by strained economic relations between our two countries.

Their stories mirror the many stories I've heard from California businesses about lost opportunities and how interconnected our commerce is with Canada.

quoted.text:
I then traveled to Ottawa, the nation's capital, to sit down with Canadian Minister for Agriculture, Heath MacDonald, and members of Parliament to discuss these issues and what can be done to mitigate the harms to both our economies until we can end them. 

The tariff wars are raising costs in the United States on everything from steel and lumber to wine bottles to the potash farmers need for their fertilizer. Between the Canadian tariffs and the war in Iran (components of fertilizer also go through the Strait of Hormuz), the input costs for farmers have gone way up. 

Without American wine on Canadian shelves, Canadians are also missing out on tens of millions of dollars in tax revenue they would obtain from selling our wine.

This gives families the time and space they need to make critical financial decisions.

text: I am horrified that a white supremacist allegedly attempted to massacre Indian Americans at a Hindu temple in Aurora. This is where the poison of anti-Indian hatred and white supremacy can lead, and we cannot wait until innocent people are killed to take it seriously. I am grateful to the coworkers who sounded the alarm and the law enforcement officers who intervened. Every American deserves to live and worship without fear, and we must stand together against hatred in all its forms. https://t.co/HbMleO2XPL
